correctness.rationale: With three candidates and two seats, unique committee is equivalent to a unique bottom-scoring candidate. After orienting a hypothetical AV {A,B} / SAV {B,C} conflict, strict comparisons imply e-d>=1, 2d-e>=1 for d=c-a and e=ab-bc, so d>=2 and e>=3: at least five ballots. Five forces 3AB+2C, yielding SAV A/B tie, not distinct UNIQUE committees. At six, d=2,e=3 and one leftover ballot: among B,AC,ABC, only B yields both unique committees, giving 3AB+B+2C. Exact independent enumeration of all anonymous compositions of n ballots into 7 nonempty approval types for n=1..6 and multinomial labeled weighting gave (both unique,distinct) at n6=(75051,360), 6 anonymous profiles one candidate-relabeling orbit. All q-rational score comparisons exact; scope fixes 3 candidates, 2 seats and nonempty ballots.
residual_risks: Existing 17-voter and 9-voter examples motivate the model; possible unindexed teaching example of six-voter profile. Anonymous count only at n=6, exactly 3 candidates and 2 seats; no general m,k or all voter-size census.
Finite checks are distinguished from symbolic proof and exhaustive finite-domain proof.

The later standard score linearization makes the strict integer comparison possible but does not imply six-ballot sharpness without the bounded diophantine argument. value.rationale: SAV was motivated as a correction to multiwinner approval bloc overrepresentation. The first electorate size where the two rules force distinct unique committees with the fewest candidates and seats, plus classification of all first conflict profiles, provides a precise natural finite threshold useful as a canonical voting example and boundary test; proof relies on nontrivial strict-score inequalities.
